page.title: PhD Math Camp
page.subtitle: Interactive companions to the math camp lectures
page.description: A short, intensive review of the mathematics used in graduate political science methods. The units below follow the lecture sequence, and each one links to its slides. Where a unit also has interactive material, its figures are reproduced as live Desmos graphs with the parameters left free, so they can be moved during class.

note.title: How these are built
note.body: The graphs are generated from Python, one script per unit, using SymPy for the algebra, SciPy and NumPy for the numerical work, and PyDesmos to emit the Desmos expressions. Every limit, root and extremum a page asserts is checked in the build, so nothing is drawn by hand and a wrong claim fails rather than shipping quietly.

units.title: Intro, Logic and Sets
units.description: Propositional and predicate logic, set operations, and applications to social science.

units.title: Relations and Functions
units.description: Relations, the vertical-line test, composition and inverses, polynomial roots, logarithms and exponentials, and monotonicity.

graphs.title: A relation that is not a function
graphs.description: Drag the slider to sweep a vertical line across the sideways parabola. It meets the curve twice for every x > 0, which is exactly what disqualifies the relation from being a function.

graphs.title: Many-to-one vs one-to-one
graphs.description: The horizontal-line test. Sweeping y = c meets the parabola twice but the line once, separating the many-to-one map from the one-to-one map.

graphs.title: Functions from ℝ to ℝ
graphs.description: The five examples from the Dimensions slide on one set of axes, for comparing growth and shape.

graphs.title: Function composition
graphs.description: Desmos composes the two functions live. The slider traces a single input through both stages, t → f(t) → g(f(t)), so the nesting is visible as two hops rather than one formula.

graphs.title: Inverse functions
graphs.description: Each function is plotted with its inverse and the line y = x. The inverses are obtained symbolically rather than typed in, and the reflection across the diagonal is the point of the picture.

graphs.title: Roots of a polynomial
graphs.description: Expanded and factored forms drawn on top of each other, with the three roots marked. The roots are found symbolically and re-checked numerically with a bracketing solver.

graphs.title: The quadratic formula
graphs.description: Sliders for a, b and c, with the discriminant and both roots entered as expressions. Moving c until the discriminant goes negative makes the root markers disappear, which is the useful thing to show.

graphs.title: Exponential and logarithmic functions
graphs.description: The reflection pair. The slider carries a point on the exponential to its mirror image on the logarithm, across y = x.

graphs.title: Monotonic functions
graphs.description: Both functions with their derivatives dotted underneath. The constant derivative and the sign change at the origin are what distinguish the monotonic case from the non-monotonic one.

graphs.title: Functions from ℝ² to ℝ
graphs.expression: x² + y² = k, 2x + y = k, x³ + 2y² = k
graphs.description: The surfaces from the slides seen from above. Desmos graphs in two dimensions, so each surface appears as its level sets, and the slider on k moves the cutting plane up and down.

units.title: Limits and Continuity
units.description: Sequences and series, convergence and divergence, the epsilon-N and epsilon-delta definitions of a limit, one-sided limits and asymptotes, continuity, and the intermediate and extreme value theorems.

graphs.title: A convergent sequence
graphs.description: The terms crowd toward 2. The slider sets ε, and the red line marks N = 1/√ε, the threshold the proof on the slide derives: every term to the right of it lies inside the ε-band.

graphs.title: A divergent sequence
graphs.description: The same picture for a sequence with no finite limit. The terms climb without settling, so no horizontal band can eventually contain them.

graphs.title: Geometric series
graphs.description: Partial sums as points, with the infinite sum a/(1−r) as a dashed line. Push the ratio r past 1 in either direction and the partial sums stop converging on it, which is exactly the |r| < 1 condition.

graphs.title: The limit of a function
graphs.description: The figure from the slide, with c on a slider. L is defined as f(c), so the dashed lines always meet on the curve as c moves.

graphs.title: The delta-epsilon definition
graphs.description: The green band is the ε-tolerance on the output, the red band the δ-window on the input, and δ is tied to ε/3 as the proof requires. Shrink ε and the red band shrinks with it, with the curve still crossing only inside the overlap.

graphs.title: A removable discontinuity
graphs.description: Factoring cancels the x − 3, leaving the line y = x + 5 everywhere except at x = 3. The open circle is the point the function never takes, though the limit there is 8.

graphs.title: A limit at infinity
graphs.description: The ratio of leading coefficients, 5/3, drawn as a horizontal asymptote. The dotted vertical line is the real root of the denominator, which SymPy locates at x = 1.

graphs.title: A vertical asymptote
graphs.description: The two one-sided limits at x = 1 run to −∞ and +∞, so the limit does not exist there. This is the fourth example from the exercises slide.

graphs.title: The squeeze theorem
graphs.description: The oscillating function is trapped between two parabolas that both tend to 0 at the origin, so it must go to 0 as well, however wildly it oscillates on the way.

graphs.title: A jump discontinuity
graphs.description: The step function from the slide. The one-sided limits are 1 and 2, so they disagree, and no value at 0 could make the function continuous.

graphs.title: Continuity of the absolute value
graphs.description: The two branches meet at the origin. Both one-sided limits equal f(0) = 0, which is the definition of continuity being satisfied at the one point where it could fail.

graphs.title: The intermediate value theorem
graphs.description: The endpoints have opposite signs, so the continuous curve has to cross zero somewhere between them. The crossing is located numerically with a bracketing solver, at x = 0.3399.

graphs.title: The extreme value theorem
graphs.description: A continuous function on a closed interval attains both bounds. The maximum is interior, at the vertex, while the minimum sits at the left endpoint.

graphs.title: The law of large numbers
graphs.description: A simulated sample, drawn with a fixed seed so the picture is reproducible. The running mean wanders early and then settles toward 0.5; the slider sets the ε-band the theorem says it eventually stays inside.

graphs.title: The Condorcet jury theorem
graphs.description: Majority-correctness probabilities computed exactly from the binomial distribution for juries of 1 to 99. Above p = 0.5 the curves climb toward certainty, quickly for p = 0.7 and slowly for p = 0.55; below it, at p = 0.45, the same logic runs the other way.

units.title: Calculus — Derivatives
units.description: The derivative, rules of differentiation, optimization, and finding extrema in one dimension.

graphs.title: Closed-form minimization of (3x − 2)²
graphs.description: Drag the slider to move the tangent point along the parabola: the tangent visibly flattens exactly at the vertex, where f′(x) = 18x − 12 crosses zero. The minimizer x* = 2/3 is solved symbolically in the build, never typed in.

graphs.title: Newton–Raphson root finding
graphs.description: Step the slider to walk Newton's method down its tangent staircase toward the root of f′(x) = x·eˣ − 16, the first-order condition from the lecture's extremum problem. Every iterate and the limit W(16) are computed and checked in the build.

graphs.title: From secant to tangent
graphs.description: Drag b toward a and watch the secant slope walk to the tangent's. The label reports the secant slope live; at b = a it would be f′(a) = 2a, the dashed line already drawn.

graphs.title: The first-order condition
graphs.description: The function from the FOC slide with its two critical points marked. Slide the tangent point along the curve: the tangent flattens exactly at the maximum (0, 7) and the minimum (2, 3), and nowhere else.

graphs.title: Concavity and risk aversion
graphs.description: The utility function from the risk-aversion slide. Move the two endpoints anywhere: the chord between them stays below the curve, which is the definition of strict concavity drawn rather than stated. The dashed curve is u′ — positive but falling.

graphs.title: An inflection point
graphs.description: The second derivative changes sign at x = 0, and the picture shows what that means: slide the tangent point through the origin and the curve crosses from one side of its tangent to the other.

graphs.title: The mean value theorem
graphs.description: The secant over [0, 4] has slope 4. Slide the tangent point until the dashed tangent runs parallel to it — that happens at c = (3 + √21)/3 ≈ 2.53, the point the theorem promises exists.

graphs.title: Taylor approximation of √x
graphs.description: The order slider adds one Taylor term at a time. At n = 3 the polynomial's value at x = 2 is 23/16 = 1.4375, the number computed on the slide, against √2 ≈ 1.4142 marked in red.

units.title: Calculus — Integrals
units.description: Integration motivated through probability: sample spaces and random variables, discrete versus continuous distributions, the relationship between the density and the CDF, and Riemann sums as approximations of area.

graphs.title: Probability as area: the uniform distribution
graphs.description: The slide's calculation, live: P(X > a) is the shaded rectangle, and its area is 1 − a. At the slide's a = 0.75 the label reads 0.25.

graphs.title: Probability as area: a triangular PDF
graphs.description: The triangular density from the slides. Move both endpoints: the shaded area is the probability, computed by Desmos as an integral. The slide's case [0.5, 1.5] gives exactly 0.5.

graphs.title: Riemann rectangles
graphs.description: The approximation from the slides, with n on a slider. At n = 10 the left sum is 0.475 — the slide's own number — and pushing n toward 100 closes the gap to the exact 0.5.

graphs.title: Accumulation is the antiderivative
graphs.description: Drag the upper limit: the shaded area grows, and the green point traces F. Where f is tall the area accumulates fast, so F is steep — the slope of F is the height of f, which is the Fundamental Theorem seen rather than proved.

graphs.title: The exponential distribution
graphs.description: Both parameters on sliders. The shaded area is the CDF at a, and the label evaluates the slide's closed form 1 − e^(−λa) — raise λ and the same probability piles up sooner.

graphs.title: Areas under the standard normal
graphs.description: P(a ≤ Z ≤ b) as shaded area, computed numerically by Desmos. The default window [−1, 1] holds 0.6827 of the mass — the first entry of the empirical rule.

graphs.title: Expectation as the center of mass
graphs.description: Slide the candidate balance point m along the axis: the label reports the torque ∫(x − m)f(x)dx, which is zero exactly at E[X] = 4/3. The mean is where the density balances.

graphs.title: The trapezoidal rule
graphs.description: The worked example from the numerical section. At n = 4 the trapezoid sum is 0.742984, the slide's value, against the exact 0.746824 — and the slider shows how fast the gap closes as n grows.

units.title: Linear Algebra
units.description: Vectors and vector operations, orthogonality, span, basis and linear independence, systems of equations, matrix operations, and an introduction to multivariate calculus.
